/**
 * What a written model can be taken to, when something can take it.
 *
 * One dialect of the three is a website's own language, and that earns a door
 * beside Copy and Save. The rule is here rather than inside the dialog so it
 * can be read and tested on its own, and so a second such dialect is one line
 * rather than a second branch in the markup.
 *
 * The value is the source's, never invented here: this only says what is known
 * about one of them.
 */

/**
 * A connection as one thing to press: the logo of its source type with the
 * state dot on it.
 *
 * One component because both the list and the collapsed strip show it, and two
 * copies of this markup would drift — pushing the column aside is meant to
 * take away the name and nothing else. What a press means stays the caller's.
 *
 * The state is said in words here rather than on the dot, which has pointer
 * events off and could never be hovered.
 */

/**
 * Whether believing the parsed choice would drop a secret the form is holding.
 *
 * A composed address never carries a secret, so taking one apart can only ever
 * answer with a way of connecting that needs none. Editing the host of a
 * connection that does need one would therefore switch the choice under the
 * user and hide what they had just typed.
 *
 * Stated about secrets and variants and not about any one source: both come
 * from the schema, and nothing here knows what a database is.
 */

/**
 * How often this grid re-reads itself, and what stops it.
 *
 * The timer is here rather than in the button because this is what owns the
 * fetch, and it runs whenever an interval is chosen — a tick that must not
 * fetch is skipped rather than queued. Two things make it skip: the tab is
 * not on screen, and the user is in the middle of something. Both matter.
 * A tab kept alive behind another one would otherwise poll the source
 * forever with nobody looking, and a poll landing while a cell is being
 * edited would throw away what was typed.
 */

/**
 * What is worth marking, and nothing else.
 *
 * A statement the source could not classify is a warning about this
 * application, not about the SQL: `unknown` means the dialect module has not
 * learnt the form, and Run will say so honestly if it is pressed.
 *
 * A relation is only marked when the metadata is complete and the schema it
 * names is one the source listed. Anything else — an alias, a CTE, a schema
 * nobody asked about, a source that answered partially — is left alone.
 */

/**
 * One captured result, in a panel of its own (D65).
 *
 * Two runs are two panels even when their SQL is the same: comparing them is
 * what the workspace's existing split and drag already do, so there is no
 * data-diff language here and no third thing to learn.
 *
 * A result does not survive a restart of the server. When it has gone the
 * table says so, and the run that produced it — which is durable — is still in
 * history.
 */

/**
 * The cached answers a committed structure change makes untrue.
 *
 * Built from what the source said changed, never from the SQL that was sent:
 * a node id is the source's, and a browser that took one apart would be
 * reading a promise D21 does not make (D66).
 *
 * `connection` is the honest wider answer for a statement that does not say
 * which node it was about, and it becomes the prefix of every key belonging to
 * this connection.
 */

/**
 * Who is waiting to be let in, and the answer.
 *
 * Beside the people who already hold a level, because it is the same question
 * one step earlier: a request is answered by an ordinary grant and by nothing
 * else (D61). Nothing at all is drawn while nobody is waiting — an empty list
 * under a heading is a heading about nothing.
 *
 * The owner's alone, like the grants: asking for the requests on a connection
 * somebody else owns is answered with 403.
 */

/**
 * Who holds a level on one connection, and what can be done about it.
 *
 * In two places — the connection's own window, where it answers the question
 * the page is about, and the Share dialog opened from a tab, where there is no
 * such page. One component because it is one question: two copies of this list
 * would be two answers to it, and the second one would be the stale one (D33).
 *
 * Only ever drawn for the owner. It asks for the grants, and asking for the
 * grants of a connection somebody else owns is answered with 403.
 */

/**
 * A resolved link waiting for the workspace to open it.
 *
 * The landing screen does the asking, because it is the screen that has to
 * explain a node that is gone (D60); what it cannot do is open a tab, since
 * the workspace is not mounted there. So the answer is left here and taken
 * once.
 *
 * A module ref and not a Pinia store: stores may not reach into the generated
 * client, and this is one screen handing another an answer it already has.
 */

/**
 * One dialog for both halves of sharing: the address, and who may follow it.
 *
 * The link is an address and carries no rights (D58), so everybody who can
 * reach the connection sees it. Grants are the owner's business (D33), so the
 * rest of the dialog appears for them alone — and the owner's sequence is one
 * movement: copy the address, add the colleague.
 *
 * Opened from a tab with a view to share, and from the connection's own window
 * without one. The link section is what differs.
 */

/**
 * One bound component per panel, kept. Three traps, each a bug once:
 *
 * - Vue tells components apart by identity, so a wrapper built afresh is a new
 *   type every render and the panel is remounted — reloading the catalog and
 *   losing the page the grid was on.
 * - Keyed by the workspace's key and not the panel's id, because an id is
 *   renamed when a console becomes a document.
 * - A component and not a render function: a functional component has no
 *   instance, so <KeepAlive> would have nothing to keep.
 */

<!-- Queries used to stand here for want of anywhere better; they are
           a command of a connection and live in the bar at the foot of the
           screen now (D69).

           No title: the tab above the panel already carries one, and saying
           it twice costs a line of a column that is a fifth of the screen.
           An icon and not a labelled button, for the same reason.

           On the left, where it stands in the strip a collapsed column leaves
           behind: pushing the column aside is meant to take the name away and
           move nothing. -->

/**
 * What a failed request says, in the three shapes the backend answers with:
 * an adapter failure as `detail: {kind, message}`, a validation failure as
 * `detail: [{loc, msg, type}]`, and a refusal a route wrote itself as
 * `detail: "a sentence"`.
 *
 * Every screen used to carry its own copy and they had drifted: only the grid
 * understood the second, and the third read as unusable until the console
 * started refusing runs, where the reason is the whole point. The fallback
 * stays the caller's, because reading rows is not saving a connection.
 */

/**
 * Whether a failed request is worth making again.
 *
 * vue-query retries everything three times, which is right for a request that
 * never arrived and wrong for one the server read and refused: it will be
 * refused again, and the retries only hold a spinner on screen first. Opening
 * a `.dump` in a file source took five seconds to say it is binary.
 *
 * The line is the status class, with the two 4xx codes that are about the
 * moment as exceptions.
 */

/**
 * Light or dark, as one button.
 *
 * The icon is what pressing it would give, not what is showing: a moon in the
 * light theme, a sun in the dark one. The tooltip says the same thing in
 * words, because an icon alone names nothing.
 *
 * In the kit rather than in a screen: it has a look, and by D11 anything with
 * a look is wrapped once here. The store behind it is the only place that
 * knows Quasar has a Dark plugin.
 */

/**
 * A tab that is switched away from takes its tooltips with it.
 *
 * A tooltip hides when the pointer leaves the button under it. Pressing a
 * button that opens another tab is the one case where that never happens: the
 * pointer does not leave, the button does. A tab that is not showing is kept
 * rather than destroyed, so nothing is unmounted and no `mouseleave` is
 * raised, and the tooltip is teleported to the body — it stayed drawn over
 * whichever tab came next until the same button was hovered and left again.
 * Being put away is a reason to hide, exactly as leaving is.
 */

/**
 * A kit component that takes its words in a slot must be given a slot.
 *
 * Vue lets an unknown attribute fall through and `vue-tsc` does not object, so
 * `<AppBanner text="..." />` compiles and renders an empty coloured bar. That
 * happened: the window showing a service's password warned about nothing, and
 * it took a screenshot to notice.
 *
 * The kit is deliberately not uniform — `AppEmptyState` takes `text`,
 * `AppBanner` takes a slot — and this is what stops that being a trap.
 */

/**
 * Where the cascade begins: the middle of the viewport.
 *
 * Not the top left, which is where this started and where it was wrong. A
 * window opening at the corner lands on top of the column it was opened from
 * and covers the very control that opens the next one — and opening a second
 * window beside the first is the whole reason these are not modal.
 *
 * The middle is a rule the engine can state without knowing what is on the
 * screen behind it, which is the only kind of rule it is allowed to have.
 */

/**
 * Where a dragged panel would land if it were released here.
 *
 * In the body the nearest edge wins and there is nothing neutral in between:
 * "beside the others" is what the strip means, and a body that meant it too
 * would be a second way to the same result, shown by a highlight describing a
 * different one. Nearness is a share of the side rather than a distance in
 * pixels — measured in pixels, the top and bottom of a wide section would
 * claim almost all of it. A tie goes to the wider side, which is the rule
 * already written for a corner. See G4.
 */

/**
 * The tab in the user's hand.
 *
 * It shows what a tab shows and nothing more: a picture of the panel would be
 * a second render of it on every movement of the pointer, and what the user
 * needs to know is which of several alike tabs they picked up — which is what
 * the subtitle is for.
 *
 * It lives in the root rather than in the section the tab came from: the
 * pointer leaves that section in the first moment of the gesture. See G2.
 */

# The lifecycle, and no state outside it.
#
#   queued → running → succeeded
#                    ↘ failed
#                    ↘ cancelled     (somebody asked it to stop)
#                    ↘ interrupted   (the process went away mid-flight)
#
# There is no `cancelling`: a task stops at its next await, and what it had
# already done to the world is a question for whoever looks at the thing it
# was doing — which is why a cancelled create is retried or removed rather
# than resumed (D84).

/**
 * Everything this source can do, and which of it these nodes admit. Asked of
 * the server: whether a node may be renamed depends on its state as well as
 * its kind, and whether an action applies to many at once only the action
 * knows. No actions at all answers 501, which is settled rather than a failure
 * to retry.
 *
 * `enabled` is for the question with no subject yet: nothing is ticked, and
 * asking about the root would answer a different question.
 */

/**
 * The columns are the list's, not each row's.
 *
 * A row takes them with `subgrid`, so names stand under names and counts
 * under counts. The one exception is a report, whose caption is a sentence
 * the source wrote rather than a measurement — left in the shared column it
 * would set the width of that column for every row in the list, so the row
 * lays itself out instead. The class is what the stylesheet keys off, so it
 * is what this checks.
 */

/**
 * Whether the head of a level says where we are.
 *
 * Read off what the level holds and never off the type of the source, which
 * is the same rule the rest of this file follows. A level that offers
 * groupings already says one thing about itself on that line, and a path of
 * one step beside it would say nothing; a level that offers none has the line
 * to itself, and drawing the path only after the first step would make it
 * appear and disappear while walking in and out.
 */

/**
 * How a source type is drawn in a list. A plain function, tested without
 * mounting anything. An unknown type gets a generic glyph rather than nothing:
 * the registry lives in the backend and gains entries without the frontend
 * being redeployed, so a missing entry here is a normal state.
 *
 * The drawings are files rather than glyphs of an icon font — a source type is
 * a product with a logo, and no font has those. Quasar loads one with the
 * `img:` prefix, served from `public/`.
 */

/**
 * A pasted connection string, taken apart into form values.
 *
 * Asked of the server for the same reason the string is composed there: the
 * rule for reading a DSN belongs to the driver. The driver also names the way
 * of connecting — a form deciding that from the presence of a password would
 * be a rule about authentication in a component that knows none.
 *
 * Nothing is opened, and nothing is stored. See the spec, V5 and V7.
 */

/**
 * The address, asked of the server whenever the values change.
 *
 * Asked while the form is still being filled in, too. The defaults put a host
 * and a port there before anything is typed, and that is already an address
 * worth showing — but composing it here would be a second implementation of a
 * grammar that belongs to the driver, and the two would differ in the quoting
 * before they differed in anything visible. So the server answers with as
 * much of the address as there is, and this end only shows what comes back.
 */

/**
 * The pages of the window that edits a connection: the groups of fields the
 * source declares, then this application's own questions, in one strip rather
 * than a strip inside a strip.
 *
 * The source's pages come first, because a connection that does not connect
 * has nothing to permit. The two this application owns are there during
 * creation too — whoever registers a source is the person who knows whether
 * anybody should write through it, and asking afterwards left it open (D66).
 */

/**
 * A placeholder per page, and a canvas only for the pages that are looked at.
 *
 * A thousand-page document then costs a thousand empty boxes rather than a
 * thousand bitmaps, which is the whole reason the renderer is worth having.
 *
 * Laid out again whenever the room changes, because a panel that is not on
 * screen has no width at all: a document opened behind another tab would
 * otherwise be drawn at its own size and scroll sideways when it is shown.
 */

/**
 * Drawing Mermaid diagrams, one at a time.
 *
 * Mermaid renders through one shared element of its own and re-reads global
 * configuration on every call, so two diagrams drawn at once take each other's
 * output: a document of four ended up with one diagram holding another's
 * contents and two holding nothing at all. Ids and a queue live here, in module
 * scope — inside a `<script setup>` block they would be per instance, which is
 * exactly the bug. See D50.
 */

/**
 * Every string that becomes DOM in a rendered document passes through here.
 *
 * Sanitising happens at two levels and the second is not a repeat of the first:
 * raw HTML written by the document's author is cleaned at token level with
 * `style` forbidden, and the assembled result is cleaned again keeping inline
 * `style` only inside KaTeX, whose layout is generated as inline styles. A
 * document can arrive from somebody else's connection through a read grant, so
 * remote resources are refused unless the reader asks for them. See D50.
 */

/**
 * Draw a reference from a column here to a column anywhere else (D106).
 *
 * One window rather than the old application's two steps — mark a column here,
 * walk somewhere else, mark another — because the second step lived in a store
 * and needed a badge in the toolbar to remind people it was waiting.
 *
 * Both ends are read the same way, as one page of the node, so the columns
 * offered are the ones the source says it can look a value up in.
 */

/**
 * What points at this relation, asked once for the relation (D110).
 *
 * A query and not a mutation, unlike following one: which keys arrive does not
 * change as the rows are paged through, and the answer decides which cells
 * offer the way back at all — so it is read when the rows are first shown and
 * kept. A source that cannot search for arriving keys answers 501, which is a
 * fact about the source and not an error to show: the marks simply do not
 * appear.
 */

/**
 * A grid that re-reads itself, and how often. Plain functions, so what is
 * offered, what is remembered and when a tick is skipped are tested without a
 * timer; the timer belongs to the component that owns the fetch.
 *
 * The pause is the interesting half: polling while somebody types into a cell
 * would throw the typing away, and polling a tab nobody looks at spends a
 * round trip per tab per interval. So a tick is "fetch unless something says
 * not to", and what says not to is one list a tooltip can also read out.
 */

/**
 * The query a 422 interrupted, held while the grid asks the source what
 * columns it has now.
 *
 * A filter and a sort name a column by name and both outlive a reload, so a
 * column renamed or dropped — here, in another tab, or by somebody else —
 * leaves a stored query the source refuses every time it is asked. Rather than
 * reading the refusal, the grid asks again without filters or sorting and
 * keeps back everything the fresh answer still knows about.
 */

/**
 * The same query with every filter and sort the relation can no longer answer
 * taken out, and the names that went.
 *
 * A filter and a sort name a column by name, and both are remembered across a
 * reload, so a column renamed or dropped leaves a stored query the source will
 * refuse forever. The columns to keep are taken from an answer the source has
 * just given rather than guessed from its refusal, which is why nothing here
 * reads an error message.
 */

/**
 * The whole tab, read off the node the source answered with.
 *
 * The answer carries a `CatalogNode` and not an id for exactly this reason
 * (D36): a tab arrived at by following a key is the same tab as one opened
 * from the catalog, so it says what it can be opened as and is drawn as
 * itself. Built here rather than in the workspace because the workspace had
 * assembled it by hand, dropped the representations, and every followed tab
 * was drawn as the logo of its source instead of as a table.
 */

/**
 * Every column this row has been offered, in the order it first appeared.
 *
 * `columns` is only what the grid shows now, and the grid can hide, show or
 * pin a column while the row is open. Seeded once per column and never
 * dropped, so a column revealed later still starts from its own rules — a
 * required one included, a boolean drafted as false — and a value already
 * typed is still sent after its column leaves the view rather than being
 * quietly discarded.
 */

/**
 * A console nobody has asked to keep, held in this browser tab and nowhere
 * else.
 *
 * Opening one writes nothing to the server; "Remember" is what makes a
 * document of it. Until then the text lives in `sessionStorage`, the only
 * place D63 allows — it dies with the tab, so this never becomes a durable
 * plaintext library of everybody's SQL. Keyed by the panel's draft id, because
 * there is no document yet.
 */

/**
 * A plan, in the three views D65 asks for, showing one selection.
 *
 * The tree is the source's own shape, the table is that tree read as a list,
 * and the raw plan is what the server prints. Choosing an operation in one is
 * choosing it in the others, because all three address it by the same id.
 *
 * Everything here is an estimate. Nothing was run, and the screen says so
 * rather than letting cost figures look like measurements.
 */

/**
 * What this console's connection is called now, not when it opened. The list
 * is asked first; the label the document carries is the fallback.
 *
 * Under confirmation this is the word a person types back, and the server
 * compares it with the name the connection has now (D66). A document that has
 * arrived answers on its own, null included: null states that the context is
 * gone (D63), and the name the tab opened with must not put a deleted
 * connection back on screen.
 */

/**
 * Where a person stands on writing through one connection.
 *
 * Keyed under the connection rather than under the queries, as the grants on
 * it are: the answer is made of the owner's policy and this person's level,
 * both of which are facts about the connection. It was under `queries` once,
 * and editing a connection then left an open console judging it by the policy
 * it used to have — every cache of a connection is dropped when it changes,
 * and this one was not among them (D66).
 */

/**
 * Choosing what this console may do, and leaving read-only on purpose (D66).
 *
 * Every document opens read-only and this is the only way out. The name of the
 * connection is typed here and checked on the server, which is where it counts.
 * Nothing is remembered: a reload opens read-only again.
 *
 * Which modes exist is the source's answer — a source that only reads (D77)
 * offers one, and one option is not a choice, so nothing is drawn.
 */

/**
 * How to reach a service from outside this application, which is not the
 * address the connection beside it holds.
 *
 * One window in two situations, separated by the password. Opened by itself
 * the moment a service becomes usable, it hands the password over once, which
 * is what the warning above it is for. Opened later from the services window
 * it shows the address and the names and no secret, which is what makes that
 * one askable as often as anybody likes.
 */

/**
 * The same thing as one line, which is what most tools actually take.
 *
 * Written by the server, because the grammar of an address belongs to the
 * source type that owns it: a screen that joined the parts itself would be a
 * second implementation of it, differing in the quoting first — putting a
 * password into one included. It carries the password in the answer that
 * hands one over and in no other, which is why this component does nothing
 * about it either way.
 */

/**
 * The commands that belong to a connection rather than to anything on screen.
 *
 * A console is written against a connection and belongs to a person, so there
 * is no node whose toolbar it could live in; it used to be squeezed in beside
 * the plus in the connections column. The bar at the foot of the screen is
 * where those go, under one rule: offered while a connection is being read and
 * that connection can do the thing. Plain functions, so the rule is tested in
 * one place rather than inferred from a row of `v-if`s.
 */

/**
   * Whether this connection could be copied out, which is two questions.
   *
   * One is about the machine — a container runtime to run `pg_dump` in and
   * somewhere to write what it produces (D87) — and the server answers it for
   * the installation. The other is about the source: only a type whose driver
   * can name a program that dumps it declares the `backup` capability, and
   * neither a file source nor a Redis server does. Both must say yes, and the
   * refusal is whichever one said no.
   */

/**
 * The library of queries, which is a person's rather than a connection's.
 *
 * In the bar with the connection's own commands because that is where a
 * person looks for it, but never disabled with them: a query outlives the
 * connection it was written against (D63), and the library has a filter of
 * its own for choosing which connection to look at. It used to be greyed out
 * until a catalog was open, which made the one place your own work lives
 * reachable only through somebody else's database.
 */

/**
 * Which column a panel belongs in.
 *
 * The engine takes this as the opaque string it places panels by, so a source
 * type that brings its own view — a topic browser, a replication monitor, a
 * query editor — is a new kind with an existing role and needs no change to
 * the layout. Roles are three because the screen has three columns; a kind is
 * what a panel is, a role is where it goes, and the two stop matching one to
 * one as soon as the second kind of table exists. See the spec, T1.
 */

/**
 * The service whose connection details are waiting to be shown, if any.
 *
 * Whichever way it was asked for: where a service listens is not something
 * anybody chose — the port is the runtime's answer, and the host is not the
 * one the connection holds — so the moment it becomes usable is the moment to
 * say so. Which service that is comes from the request; when it is ready
 * comes from the services query, because a job event says something moved and
 * the query says what it moved to (D81).
 */

/**
 * Whether the first level has come back.
 *
 * What the head shows follows from what the level holds, and before the first
 * answer it holds nothing — which reads the same as a level with nothing to
 * filter by. Deciding then would draw the path for one round trip and take it
 * away again on every source that does have groupings. `loading` cannot stand
 * in for this: it goes up on every later reload too, and the head would blink
 * each time.
 */

/**
 * The node this catalog was told to point at.
 *
 * Taken from the workspace rather than passed in: the panel may have been
 * opened by the very press that asked for the pointing, so `immediate` is what
 * catches the target that was set before this existed.
 *
 * Where the node lives is asked of the source, which is the only party that
 * knows what its own ids are made of — see D21. Nothing here takes one apart.
 */

/**
 * A layer is a meaning, as a colour is: the window engine once lost to a
 * sticky table heading that declared `1`, and the drop zone lost to the same
 * heading afterwards.
 *
 * This reads `.vue` files, where every component style lives. A `.css` file
 * cannot be read from a unit test at all — `import.meta.glob` and `?raw` both
 * hand back the name and an empty string — so the scale's own order is checked
 * in the browser, by the Playwright scenario about a sticky heading.
 */

/**
 * What one chosen color turns into: a surface, the text that stays readable
 * on it, and the same color said quietly.
 *
 * Three and not one, because a color is used for two different jobs. A tab is
 * filled with it and needs to know what to write on it; a row that is merely
 * open is marked by a wash of it and keeps the text color it had, the way
 * `--dp-selected-quiet` is the quiet half of `--dp-selected`. Both are decided
 * here so that a screen asks for the meaning and never mixes a color itself.
 */

/**
 * Where to put a window that is being opened.
 *
 * Offset from the last one opened rather than from the number of open
 * windows: closing one in the middle would otherwise send the next new window
 * backwards, onto a place that is still taken.
 *
 * The cascade restarts once it would walk off the screen, so a long session
 * does not push windows out of reach before `clamp` has to rescue them.
 */

/**
 * Floating windows over the application. The engine knows nothing about what a
 * window holds — an id, a size, a look and a component — the same split that
 * keeps `shared/workspace` free of any knowledge of panels.
 *
 * Windows are not modal, and that is the requirement: one connection is read
 * while another is filled in beside it. What modality would have given is
 * replaced by asking before a window with unsaved changes is closed, which is
 * the feature's business and not the engine's.
 */

/**
 * 2: sections gained a role and the right to stay empty. A layout written
 * before that is one section holding everything, so restoring it would leave
 * the user without the columns the screen now promises.
 *
 * 3: a data tab carries the connection it came from, so that it can say whose
 * it is and draw the icon of its source before the list of connections has
 * been read. A layout written under 2 holds tabs that cannot. Refused whole,
 * like any other foreign version — see the spec, T6 and P8.
 */

/**
 * Move the border between `children[before]` and `children[after]`.
 *
 * Two indices rather than one and its successor: a section with nothing to
 * show is off the screen, so the two the user sees either side of a border are
 * not neighbours in the tree, and everything between them keeps its width.
 *
 * Sizes are percentages and the limit is pixels, so the caller converts — this
 * function knows nothing about the screen.
 */

/**
 * Whether a section is on the screen at all.
 *
 * `pinned` keeps a *role* on the screen rather than one particular section:
 * a section split off another inherits the role (P2), so a pinned column can
 * be left holding nothing while its role is served by the section beside it —
 * and an empty view that says "pick a table to read it here" next to an open
 * table promises what has already been done. The engine still reads no role:
 * it compares two opaque strings and counts panels. See P4.
 */

/**
 * Light or dark. Pinia, because the server knows nothing about it (D6). Two
 * states and not three: "as the system says" is what answers before anything
 * is chosen, and offering it back would be a state whose only job is to return
 * to the default.
 *
 * The one place that names Quasar's Dark plugin. It puts `body--dark` on the
 * document and `shared/ui/theme.css` hangs every colour of ours off the same
 * class, so the kit and the screens turn over on one event rather than two.
 */

# How a source's catalog is best shown. Not a decoration: a catalog walked one
# level at a time and a catalog expanded in place are different screens, and
# which one a source wants is a property of the source rather than of the
# screen. PostgreSQL has thousands of relations under a schema and is walked;
# a Redis key space is bounded and its leaves hold structure, so it is a tree
# that opens where you are.
#
# A closed set, so a screen switching on it cannot meet a value it has no
# panel for, and read off the type rather than branched on by name — a screen
# that said `if adapterType === "redis"` would be the old application (D62).

/**
 * The groupings a form may send, in the order the level lists them.
 *
 * A source's own machinery is left out: `pg_catalog` is a real schema and is
 * shown in the catalog for that reason, but offering it as a place to move a
 * table into is offering something every source refuses. Ids and not names —
 * the value travels back to the source that issued it, and nothing here reads
 * what one is made of (D21).
 */

/**
 * The fields of a form, with a field that names a grouping made a choice.
 *
 * The schema cannot carry the list: groupings belong to one connection and the
 * schema is declared by the adapter class, so the server says what the field
 * means and the client fills in what this connection has. Nothing is changed
 * where there is nothing to choose from — a select with no options is a dead
 * end, and the name can still be typed.
 */

/**
 * The selection as a set, or nothing when it is not one.
 *
 * The root of a connector travels as null and has no id to put in a list, so
 * a selection holding one is not a set. One function because two callers must
 * agree: what is previewed as a set and what is sent as a set are the same
 * selection, and a disagreement would show a person the consequences of a
 * request that is never made.
 */

/**
 * The tables inside one node: the sheets of a workbook.
 *
 * The same query the catalog itself makes, by the same key, so a tab that
 * offers the sheets of a file the catalog has already listed reads nothing
 * again. Only nodes that open as a table are offered — a container of tables
 * holds nothing else today, and a listing that quietly included something
 * unopenable would be a switcher with a dead entry in it.
 */

/**
 * A click is on the whole row, wherever in it the pointer landed. With a
 * selection bound the tree selects on a click and does nothing else, which is
 * why opening a branch is here: a name is a bigger target than the arrow
 * beside it, and reaching for that arrow is what made this tree feel stiff.
 *
 * Nothing here touches the selection — a second answer arriving a moment
 * before the tree's own turned every click into a select and an unselect.
 */

/**
 * A path of nodes read as a place on the screen. The server answers with every
 * node from the root down, and those are not crumbs: in PostgreSQL a schema is
 * a node of the path but a grouping on the screen, while a directory is a
 * level one walks into. `roleOf` decides which.
 *
 * The root is not in the path — it is the connector, and the level puts its
 * own crumb there.
 */

/**
   * Every name must exist in the Material Icons set the application bundles.
   *
   * A name that only exists in the newer Material Symbols is not a missing
   * picture: `q-icon` draws the literal word, which overflows its 18px box and
   * covers the tick box beside it. That is how `monitoring` was found, and
   * only a browser noticed. The bundled list keys each icon camel-cased, so
   * `grid_on` is `matGridOn`.
   */

/**
 * What the catalog does with a node, decided by its kind.
 *
 * This table is the whole reason the screen never asks what type of source it
 * is looking at. A schema is a grouping rather than a place — it belongs in
 * the filter above the list, not in the list — while a directory is a place
 * one walks into, and a table is something to open. Adding a source type that
 * brings databases or namespaces means adding a line here, not a branch.
 */

/**
 * Which groupings are on before the user has chosen.
 *
 * What the source named, if it named one: a Redis connection is written with a
 * database number in it, and only the source has read it. Otherwise all the
 * real ones while there are few and the first while there are many — three
 * schemas is a database somebody wants to see into, forty is a page nobody
 * asked for. System groupings stay off, and can be ticked.
 */

/**
 * Choosing a chart over rows somebody else read (D35).
 *
 * Controlled, like the tabular surface of D24: it is given columns, rows and
 * where they start, and knows nothing about where they came from. A relation's
 * page and a captured query result are two controllers of the same thing, and
 * this is what keeps the pickers, the suggestions and the persistence in one
 * place rather than in two that drift.
 */

/**
 * The first of the two steps of adding a connection: which kind of source.
 *
 * A window of its own rather than a step inside the form. The two are
 * different sizes — a grid needs 900px, a form 520 — and one component that
 * changed width between steps would carry two roles as well. Editing an
 * existing connection then opens the form directly, with nothing to say about
 * a catalog it never came from. See the spec, K3.
 */

/**
 * Finding a source type in the catalog. Plain functions, tested without
 * mounting anything.
 *
 * Lexical only, and what is matched comes from the server: a type gains
 * searchable words by gaining a capability, not by anyone remembering to write
 * one down. The old application shipped an embedding model to the browser to
 * search 84 hand-written descriptions.
 */

/**
 * Whether an answer from this connection could ever be older than the read.
 *
 * Two ways to be no, and both count: a source that never opted into caching
 * keeps nothing whatever its owner typed, and an owner who chose to keep
 * nothing meant it. Unknown counts as no as well — the lists arrive a moment
 * after the panel, and a mark that appears is easier to read than one that
 * appears and goes away (D105).
 */

/**
 * The connection string of a draft, composed by the server.
 *
 * A request while the form is being typed into, and that is the price of the
 * rule living in one place: the driver knows how its own address is built,
 * and a template filled in on the client would be the same statement made
 * twice. It opens no connection, so the cost is the round trip and nothing
 * more. A source that has no such address answers 501. See the spec, O8.
 */

/* Open somewhere, and the one being read. The full mark is written after the
   quiet one so that it wins where both apply.

   In the connection's own colour where it has one, so a row and the tabs it
   opened are visibly one thing. The row being read takes the colour whole and
   the text that contrasts with it; a row merely open takes a wash of it. A
   connection with no colour is marked just the same, in the plain colour its
   tabs are filled with and in the quiet half of that — the mark is the same
   mark either way, and only the colour of it is a choice. */

/**
 * What state a connection is in, and how to say it in words.
 *
 * Two readers: the dot takes the tone, the icon around it takes the words for
 * its tooltip. The dot cannot carry the tooltip itself — it is drawn on top of
 * the icon with pointer events off, so nothing would ever hover it.
 *
 * Pure, so the rule is tested without mounting anything.
 */

/**
 * What the form held when it was last loaded or saved.
 *
 * `dirty` is the answer to "does it still hold that", not a flag something
 * sets. As a flag it was set by the window filling itself in: loading a
 * connection assigns the name and the values, which is a change to watch, and
 * every window then asked whether to discard changes nobody had made. A
 * question asked every time teaches people to answer it without reading.
 */

/**
 * Shown, and not editable.
 *
 * A grant is access to the source, not to the record of how to reach it: the
 * options and the credentials stay the owner's. The form is disabled rather
 * than hidden, because seeing what one is connected to — which host, which
 * database — is part of what reading it means. Testing the connection stays
 * available: it opens nothing this window does not already read.
 */

/**
 * An address typed into the URL box, taken apart into the fields.
 *
 * The box keeps no answer of its own: what is typed goes to the driver, the
 * driver produces fields, and the fields compose the string that comes back.
 * A password typed into the box therefore lands in the password field and
 * leaves the box. Delayed because it is a request, and not made at all for
 * text the server itself composed.
 */

/**
   * The words this editor offers, from two places at once.
   *
   * The caller's — schemas, relations, columns, parameters — and whatever the
   * language itself completes, which for SQL is its keywords. Asked for here
   * rather than left to the default source because the two have to appear in
   * one list, and a qualified name and a keyword do not start at the same
   * place in the text.
   */

/**
 * What an `echarts` fence inside a document may draw.
 *
 * This is a wider vocabulary than the chart panel's (D35), and deliberately so:
 * a chart built over a connection's rows is composed by the application from a
 * closed set of choices, while a fence is a picture its author already drew.
 * The set is the one the documents this viewer was ported from actually use.
 * It is loaded with the block, not with the application.
 */

/**
 * Correct what Mermaid draws once labels are native SVG text.
 *
 * Without HTML labels every edge label is given an opaque `rect.background`,
 * which reads as a box drawn around `yes` and `no` on a flowchart. A subgraph's
 * frame also comes out in Mermaid's own palette rather than this application's.
 * The rules are scoped by the diagram's id: a `<style>` inside inline SVG is a
 * stylesheet of the whole page.
 */

/**
 * A rectangle of cells read back out of clipboard text.
 *
 * Returns null for text that is not a rectangle — rows of differing widths —
 * because a block that is not one has no unambiguous landing place, and
 * guessing where the short rows stop is worse than saying so.
 *
 * Empty text is not a rectangle either: there is nothing to paste.
 */

/**
 * Whether a followed reference decided this tab's query.
 *
 * The stored query of a relation is restored the first time the source names
 * its columns, which happens after the panel is opened — so without this the
 * remembered filters would land on top of the ones somebody just navigated
 * by. What was navigated to is stored in its turn, exactly as a filter the
 * user typed is: the tab keeps showing what it was last asked to show.
 */

/**
 * The shared view this tab was opened by, applied once the source has named
 * its columns.
 *
 * Both halves of a link go through `reconcileGridState`, which a tab restored
 * from storage also uses, so a column the relation no longer has is dropped in
 * one place and said rather than silently missing (D60). Waiting for the
 * columns first: a filter naming a gone column would be sent and refused.
 */

/**
 * What an applied filter says, the value included.
 *
 * The value is the half that used to be missing. A page filtered to nothing
 * read as broken, because the condition on screen named the column and the
 * operator and left out the one thing that explained the empty result — and a
 * predicate that arrived by following a reference was never typed by anybody,
 * so there was nowhere else to see it (D106).
 */

/**
 * A copied line read back into the fields of a row being inserted.
 *
 * Positional, and that is exact rather than lucky: the grid and the insert row
 * are built from the same ordered list of visible columns, so the nth value of
 * a copied line belongs to the nth field. What the source fills itself — an
 * identity, a generated column — is left out rather than refused, since a
 * copied row always carries those and refusing would make the gesture useless.
 */

/**
 * What one row holds for every column of one reference.
 *
 * Every column of the key, whatever the row has in it — a missing value is
 * sent as null rather than left out, because what an absent key names is the
 * source's answer and not this file's guess. Nothing is returned at all when
 * the page does not carry one of the columns, which is a page read before the
 * relation changed.
 */

/**
 * Turning a selection of rows into what a source-declared command takes.
 *
 * A row command (D70) names one column as the thing that identifies a row —
 * `pid` for a list of server processes. The grid holds a page of text and a
 * set of selected row numbers, and this is the whole of the translation
 * between them. Nothing here is keyed by the name of a command: which column
 * to read comes from the answer that offered it.
 */

/**
 * The ways in and out of one row, wherever a row is shown: the key that leads
 * away (D36) and the keys landing on it that lead back (D110).
 *
 * Written once so the grid and the row view cannot drift into two answers
 * about which cell offers what — which is how the old application ended up
 * copying a constraint onto every column it touched. What differs between the
 * callers is only which columns are on screen.
 */

/**
 * What the editor offers, and what it dares say is wrong.
 *
 * Plain data in, plain data out, so both rules can be tested without an editor.
 * Both are conservative on purpose (D65): completion offers what the source has
 * said it has, and a mark appears only where this application actually knows
 * something — limited metadata produces a status, never a red line under a
 * relation that exists.
 */

/**
 * Which of the three places this panel is showing.
 *
 * One state rather than two flags that overlap. Queries are what somebody is
 * writing, Trash is what they deleted, and History is what actually ran — the
 * same person's three questions about their own queries, in the one place they
 * look for them (D63). As two booleans, pressing Trash while looking at
 * History did nothing and the button had to be greyed out to say so.
 */

/**
 * One console: a document above, what it produced below (D65).
 *
 * Run follows the convention without importing an IDE shell. Ctrl+Enter runs
 * the selection or the statement under the caret and never falls back to the
 * whole document; Ctrl+Shift+Enter is the deliberately different command that
 * runs all of it. Where the statements are is the source's answer rather than
 * this screen's — the browser does not split SQL (D62).
 */

/**
 * The bar answers as soon as a run does, not at the next poll.
 *
 * The transaction is asked every five seconds because it also expires without
 * anybody touching it. But a run that has just finished is a change this
 * screen already knows about, and a commit preview still saying "0 changing
 * statements" under a statement that has visibly succeeded is the one moment
 * it must not be behind (D66).
 */

/**
 * One captured result, read as a table (D64).
 *
 * The controlled tabular surface of D24 with a different controller behind it:
 * a query result has no update, insert, delete, reference, structure or import
 * command, because an arbitrary projection has no row identity to act on. What
 * it does have is paging, filtering and ordering — over the snapshot, which
 * the empty state and the download both say.
 */

/**
 * Structure changes in the console: what to rehearse, what to say, what to
 * re-read afterwards (D66).
 *
 * Plain functions rather than component code, so each of the three can be
 * tested without a database behind it or a panel around it. None of them
 * decides whether a change may be made — that is the server's answer, four
 * times over — and none of them builds a node id.
 */

/**
 * Whether the question is on screen: a writing mode, chosen while writes are
 * locked and while the connection admits them at all.
 *
 * Read from all three, and not set when the mode changes. What the connection
 * allows can change under an open console — its owner may close writing on it
 * or open it again — and a flag written on the way in kept asking, or kept not
 * asking, whatever the connection said afterwards (D66).
 */

/**
 * One row, read downwards: every column on screen at once with what the source
 * says about each beside the value.
 *
 * The same page the grid is reading, asked for by the same key, so opening a
 * row costs no request and the two cannot disagree. Which row is a position in
 * that page and not a handle — a handle exists only where the source can
 * version a row (D25), and walking to the next is a question about the page.
 */

/**
 * The same, with the password, asked for exactly once.
 *
 * `staleTime: Infinity` and no retry, because this is not a read: the server
 * stamps the row as handed over and refuses the second ask. A refetch would
 * turn the one answer into a refusal on the screen of the person who was
 * being told it — which is why the cached answer has to outlive the window
 * being closed and opened again in the same session.
 */

/**
 * What this server is running. A service is the container a database lives in;
 * the connection beside it is how that database is used.
 *
 * The only place a service's life can be ended, taking the volume and
 * therefore the data with it. It lives in a window rather than above the
 * connections: a service is looked at while something is being done to it and
 * not otherwise, and that column is where every connection goes (D69).
 */

/**
 * Taking a service away takes its data with it, so it is asked about first.
 *
 * And the connection it made is a second question in the same breath, ticked
 * by default: a connection to a database that no longer exists works for
 * nobody. Not decided here either way, because it may be shared and it may be
 * named in somebody's query history (D84) — so it is asked rather than
 * assumed, and a service that never became one is not asked about at all.
 */

/**
 * What to say about the password.
 *
 * Four situations, and the one that matters is the first: a password this
 * server made up is being said for the only time it will ever be said, and a
 * person who closes this window without copying it has lost it. Said before
 * the rows rather than after them, because a warning under something the
 * reader has already closed is not a warning.
 */

/**
 * The request a filled-in form means. A plain function, so what "automatic"
 * leaves out is a thing with a test: an automatic start carries nothing at
 * all, including the name.
 *
 * A value typed into a field the template did not open is dropped rather than
 * sent, because the server refuses one and a form that sends what will be
 * refused is a form that lies.
 */

/**
 * What a password has to be, said the same way the server says it.
 *
 * Printable characters with no space among them, because the string becomes an
 * environment variable in a container specification, an argument on a command
 * line and part of a connection string. The server refuses one that is not;
 * this is here so the refusal is read before the button is pressed rather
 * than after.
 */

/**
 * Two ways to start a database, differing in how many questions are asked.
 *
 * Automatic asks none, not even the name: somebody who has not been asked for
 * a name has not got one in mind, and asking is the difference between a
 * demonstration and a form. Chosen asks what is a person's to decide — the
 * name, the names inside it, the port and the password. What runs is the
 * template's either way: no image, no command, no path (D80).
 */

/**
 * Where a shared link lands.
 *
 * The asking happens here rather than in the workspace because this is the
 * screen that has to explain the answers: no standing on the connection, a
 * node that is gone, a connection switched off. What it cannot do is open a
 * tab, so a link that resolves is left for the workspace and this screen steps
 * out of the way. See D60.
 */

/**
 * The format's own facts.
 *
 * The switch is exhaustive: a format added to the union on the server is a
 * type error here until somebody decides what a reader should be told about
 * it — the reason the facts travel as a union rather than as pairs of strings
 * the source wrote. Two of its members are a dataset's, and are printed by the
 * function that already prints one.
 */

/**
 * Which catalog the user is looking at, read off the layout itself.
 *
 * With one catalog open, "the first catalog panel there is" was the same
 * answer. With several it is the one opened earliest rather than the one being
 * read, so the question is put to the tree: the sections that take catalogs,
 * the focused one first, and its active tab. Nothing is kept beside the tree
 * that could disagree with it. See P7.
 */

/**
 * The bar at the foot of the screen: what can be done to the open connection —
 * a command that belongs to a connection and to no node in it, which until now
 * was squeezed in beside the plus in the connections column.
 *
 * Which connection is not written here. It is already said in the column of
 * connections and on the tab of the catalog, and a third copy took the room
 * the commands want; each tooltip names it where a button leaves doubt (D69).
 */

/**
 * What this server is running for this person, which is not about a
 * connection at all.
 *
 * So it stands apart from the rest of the bar rather than among them. While a
 * job is working the button says the step it has reached: once the dialog
 * that asked for a service has closed, this is the only place a start is
 * visible (D81).
 */

/**
 * The row of commands a panel keeps about itself (D112): the way back to its
 * node in a catalog, and the re-read. The way out of a window is not here — it
 * is about the frame, and stands in the window's own bar.
 *
 * The re-read absorbed the freshness badge, which stood beside it as a control
 * of its own and re-read the source when pressed. It is a mark now, "Live" or
 * a clock, riding above the reload; the age is in what is said on hover (D105).
 */

/**
 * The workspace: connections, catalogs and node-specific work, side by side.
 *
 * Three columns that are always there, because each one is a role rather than
 * a place something was once dragged to: `accepts` puts a newly opened panel
 * in the right column, and `pinned` keeps that column when the last thing in
 * it is closed. Everything else is the user's — widths, which tabs are open,
 * and a data tab torn off into a section of its own. See the spec, T5.
 */

/**
 * Ask this server to start one, instead of filling a form about somebody
 * else's.
 *
 * The catalog closes and one question is asked — what to call it — because a
 * person who starts two databases needs to tell them apart. Nothing is waited
 * for after that: the answer is a job, and where it has got to is shown
 * beside the connections until it becomes one (D83).
 */

/**
   * Open the target of a reference and hand its tab the predicate.
   *
   * Two steps rather than one because the tab may already be open: opening it
   * brings it forward, and what it is to show is left where the tab picks it
   * up. The tab is the relation, as every rows tab is — following a key from
   * two different rows is the same table with a different question asked of
   * it, and the answer to the last one is what a tab shows.
   */

/**
 * One chain for everything that moves the level.
 *
 * The first read and a pointing that arrived together with the panel would
 * otherwise race, and whichever lost would leave the catalog somewhere the
 * user did not ask for — the pointing is what opened the panel, so the two
 * start in the same breath. They run in the order they are queued here, which
 * is why the first read is queued in setup rather than on mount.
 */

/**
 * Where we are, in the clipboard.
 *
 * The source's own name for this level and not the trail as it is drawn: the
 * crumbs are labels a reader follows, while the id is the string that names
 * the place — for a file source, the path below the root, which is what the
 * root's owner types elsewhere. Nothing to copy at the root: the root is the
 * connection, and it is never named to a client.
 */

/**
 * What this tab is actually showing, which is not always the node it is on.
 *
 * A workbook opens as its first sheet, so a tab opened on the file is reading
 * a sheet — and everything it offers about what it shows has to be that
 * sheet's. The structure button was the file's answer, and a file that holds
 * tables states no columns of its own: the button appeared only once somebody
 * had switched sheets, which is the moment the node stopped being the file.
 */

/**
 * The server refusing who we are, as opposed to refusing what we asked.
 *
 * 401 only. 403 used to be on this list, back when it was what an unusable
 * token got; it now means the caller is known and this is not theirs — too low
 * a level on a connection, or an administrator's route. Signing somebody out
 * for that would end the session over a button they should not have been
 * offered. See D33.
 */

/**
 * What the server answered with, or null when nothing arrived from it.
 *
 * The status is part of the answer and not only of the failure: a source
 * saying 501 to a capability is stating something about itself, and a request
 * that never arrived is stating nothing at all. Telling the two apart is the
 * difference between a row that is absent because it has no meaning and a row
 * that vanished because the network blinked.
 */

/**
 * Keep tabs connected to the same server on the same session.
 *
 * A 401 already sends the user to the login page, but signing out elsewhere
 * produces no 401 at all: the token stays valid on the server until it
 * expires, so this tab would keep working with a session the user believes
 * they ended. The browser reports the change through the `storage` event,
 * which fires only in the tabs that did not make it.
 */

/**
 * Whether what is on screen was read now or kept, and how old it is (D105).
 *
 * Two caches sit between a source and a grid and neither can answer alone: the
 * browser knows when the reply arrived, the server knows how long it had been
 * sitting there first. The server sends its part and this adds the browser's.
 *
 * Plain functions, so what is drawn can be tested without mounting anything.
 */

/**
 * The application's one socket.
 *
 * A module-level instance because in a browser tab the module and the
 * application are the same thing — there is no second application to hand a
 * second socket to, and the server keys what it pushes by user rather than by
 * connection. Opening is still lazy: nothing connects until a screen asks to
 * watch something.
 */

/**
 * One property, with an optional field's two branches folded back into it.
 *
 * `int | None` reaches the client as `anyOf: [{type: "integer", …}, {type:
 * "null"}]`, and the bounds go with the branch rather than staying beside it.
 * Folding the non-null branch back in makes it an ordinary field with
 * `required: false`, which is what the rest of this module knows how to draw.
 * Anything else with an `anyOf` fails loudly below.
 */

/**
       * Everything a variant shows, in the order its model declared it, the
       * choice among them.
       *
       * The order is the server's statement and not this function's: a model
       * puts the choice under the address by declaring it there, and a form
       * that gathered all the shared fields first would override that with a
       * rule of its own.
       */

/**
 * A stored secret, shown as a stand-in until the user means to replace it.
 *
 * The alternative — a placeholder — reads as an empty field, and an empty
 * field beside a saved connection says the password was lost. This says there
 * is one and that it is not being shown; touching it empties the field and
 * whatever is typed then replaces it. A field left untouched reports nothing,
 * and the server keeps what it has.
 */

/* The rows scroll, the header does not. Quasar builds the table out of nested
   elements, so the height has to be handed down to the one that scrolls.

   The background belongs here rather than on a descendant: the class lands on
   the same element Quasar calls `q-table__container`, which is what carries
   the table's own card — white, and #1d1d1d in the dark theme. Over a panel
   that is `--dp-surface` that made three colours out of one column: the panel,
   the card on it, and the sticky heading on that. A table filling a panel is
   not a card; it takes the surface it was put on. */

/**
 * One command of a window's own, drawn in its bar beside the size controls.
 *
 * What a window *is* rather than what it holds: returning a detached panel to
 * the workspace belongs with minimize, maximize and close, because all four
 * are about the frame and none of them is about the rows inside it. The engine
 * knows only the icon, the words and what to call — which feature supplies it
 * and what pressing it does are none of its business (D112).
 */

/**
   * What this window *is*, as opposed to what it shows.
   *
   * Fixed for as long as the window lives, while `id` may change — a saved
   * draft becomes the window of the connection it created. Keying the list by
   * `id` unmounted the window at that moment and mounted a fresh one: the
   * form reset itself, and the close that followed the save was delivered to
   * an instance that no longer existed.
   */

/**
 * Which place in a strip of tabs the pointer is between: the index the dragged
 * panel takes if released now, 0 before the first and `tabs.length` after the
 * last. A tab is claimed by whichever half the pointer is in, so the mark
 * moves at its middle rather than its edge.
 *
 * The rectangles are the tabs that are drawn, and the one in the hand is not
 * among them, so this is already an index into the strip as it will be.
 */

/**
 * The highlight shows where the panel will end up, not which zone the pointer
 * happens to be in.
 *
 * A tab joining the others ends up in the head, so the head lights up; a whole
 * panel lit for that describes a result that will not happen. The one case
 * where the whole section is honest is the section that holds nothing: the
 * panel really will fill it. See G5.
 */

/**
 * How much of a split each of its sections takes, once the ones with nothing
 * to show are off the screen.
 *
 * A column that is on screen keeps the width it was given: `sizes` in the tree
 * are never touched, exactly as they are not touched when a column is

# What an action changes: an explicitly selected node, a shown place's
# children, or the catalog level itself. A client has to tell the three apart
# to know what to send an action, and reading it off the names would mean
# teaching the client every action that is ever added (D56).

# How much of an upload is taken at a time. Big enough that a large file is
# not a million round trips, small enough that a refused one is caught long
# before it is all in memory. Beside `FilePayload` rather than in one adapter,
# because both sources that read an upload read it the same way.

# Declared beside applies_to because it is the same sort of statement: one
    # says which kinds of node an action makes sense for, the other says what
    # of that node it changes. `level` is the catalog level itself, kept apart
    # from a selected grouping whose children happen to be shown in it.

# What a caller must hold on the connection to run this. Declared on the
    # class beside `destructive` because it is the same sort of statement, and
    # defaulting to `write` so that an action which says nothing about itself
    # is not thereby free to anyone who can read.

# Storing is conditional on this load still being the one the
            # flight table names. Invalidation removes it from there, and that
            # alone is what stops a read begun before a mutation from putting
            # its stale answer back after it.

# Forgetting the flight does two things at once, and both matter: a
            # call begun after this mutation cannot coalesce with an older read,
            # and that older read can no longer store what it returns, because
            # storing requires still being named here.

# Whether this node also answers `relation-model`. Said by the source
    # rather than worked out by the client from the kind: a PostgreSQL schema
    # is not describable while its tables are, and among files only the ones
    # that declare their own columns are (D51).

# Whether this node also answers `node-summary`: how big, since when, what
    # it may be opened as, and what its format states about itself. Said by the
    # source for the reason `describable` is said by it — a client that worked
    # it out from the kind would be deciding what a source can answer (D75).

# The kinds themselves, as a closed set. A route needs to speak about the kind
# of a node without holding one — deciding which actions a directory admits,
# for instance — and a bare string there would let a typo through silently.
# The test that this matches the union keeps the two from drifting apart.

# TypeAdapter builds a validator and a schema on construction, and both are
# asked for on the path of an ordinary request. Keyed by identity rather than
# by equality: a schema is a module-level object, and a FieldInfo inside an
# Annotated union is not hashable, so a dict cannot hold one as a key.

# Why this source will not carry the statement out, when it will not. The
    # vocabulary of structure changes is closed and is dialect knowledge, so
    # the source names what falls outside it rather than the module that runs
    # statements keeping a second list of its own (D66).

# `nodes` names exactly what changed. `connection` is the honest answer
    # when the statement does not say: `DROP INDEX s.i` names the index, and
    # which relation it was on is not in the text. Everything about the
    # connection is re-read rather than a node being guessed at.

# Which way a reference is being followed. Said rather than worked out from the
# name: a constraint name is unique within a relation and not within a schema,
# so a key of this relation and a key landing on it can be called the same
# thing (D110).

# What a screen may switch on. A title is written to be read and may be
# reworded tomorrow; a code is a promise. Only what a screen has actually had
# to ask about carries one, so this grows when a question is asked rather than
# in advance — and everything else stays what it is, something to read.

# The three fields below are relational vocabulary. A source that has no
    # such notion leaves them out rather than filling them in: a Parquet file
    # sits in no schema, is owned by no role and is not "permanent" in the
    # sense a table is.

# A third gate, for the third question. The three admit different kinds of
    # relation — a materialized view can be indexed but has no constraints, a
    # child partition takes its columns from its parent but holds constraints
    # of its own — so one flag could only be wrong about two of them.

# No third ceiling on the product of the two: what a whole file may
        # weigh is a question for whoever supplies the rows, and the one place
        # that does today refuses a file over its own byte limit while it is
        # still arriving.

# How long this kind of source keeps its own answers, so the form that
    # offers to re-time a connection can say what it would be changing, and
    # say plainly when there is nothing to change. Null when the source keeps

# A schema count is bounded, a directory is not. Beyond this the listing fails
# rather than being cut short: pagination of catalog children does not exist
# yet, and pretending a directory is smaller than it is would be a lie of the
# kind the old catalog told when it answered with the parent directory.

# What each of the engine's statement types is, in the platform's vocabulary.
# Keyed by name rather than by enum member so that a type a later version of
# the engine adds arrives as `unknown` and is refused, instead of matching some
# neighbouring number.

# The first sheet somebody would see on opening it in a

# What can be read out of an archive entry: every viewer a bounded expansion

# are streamed by range, and a nested archive would need a reader inside a

# What reading inside files may cost. The first is per file — a file larger
# than this is somebody's data set rather than something they are grepping —
# and the second is for the whole search, so that a folder of a thousand large
# files stops rather than running for minutes.

# A match carries the folder it sits in twice over: the opaque id the

# The name decides first, and only a match is built

# The destinations are the source's own groupings, and only the source can

# How many rows one loaded file may bring. More than this is a durable job
# with progress and cancellation, which is Phase 4. Refused rather than
# truncated: the reader handed over a whole file and would have no way of

# How much of the file is read before it is refused. The rows are parsed from

# memory of one request; the row ceiling alone would not, since one row can be
# as long as the whole file.

# Which report admits which commands. `applies_to` speaks about kinds, and
# every report is a report: one of them is about extensions and another about

# No name in the statement, for the reason D39 gives: PostgreSQL

# No CASCADE, the rule D27 set for a column: an outside dependency

        # standing on this unique constraint is such a dependency, and it is

# A single catalog expression is clipped before it crosses the connection.
# PostgreSQL's left() counts characters rather than bytes, so this is the
# smallest character limit that still permits every valid UTF-8 answer up to
# MAX_DDL_BYTES; the final byte prefix is the authoritative response bound.

# Both, and whatever the statement was: a create or a drop changes what
        # the schema holds, and an alter changes what is inside the relation.

        # dialect for no gain, and the wrong answer would be a stale screen.

# The same constraints read from the other end: everything whose `confrelid`
# is this relation. A relation everything points at — a `users` of a large
# schema — can be named by dozens, and a menu is not a report, so the answer
# has a ceiling and the query carries it (D110).

# How a row is named. The key where there is one, because a physical
    # position is invalidated wholesale by anything that rewrites the table;
    # its place where there is not, because that is better than refusing to

# An id in the reports' own namespace that names no report is wrong

# How long a rehearsal waits for a lock before giving up. Short on purpose: a
# preview that queues behind somebody else's transaction is a preview that
# holds the person looking at it, and the honest answer is that it is blocked
# rather than a spinner (D66).

# A relation the server owns is described in full and changed by

# The named volume personal storage lives in, so that a program run in

    # subject to know what to do — which backup to write back, say. Never a

# Which of them were asked to stop. Without this, a task that ends in

# What that document is called, when it is still there and has a name. The
    # id alone made history a second list of SQL beside the library, with no

# --- history ----------------------------------------------------------------
#
# D63: a view of accepted immutable runs, kept for as long as their owner
# chooses. Deleting leaves nothing behind — there is no audit copy.

# A container that stops on its own comes back, and one this application asked
# to stop stays stopped. `unless-stopped` is exactly that promise, and it is
# written here rather than in a template because it is a rule about every
# service this server keeps, not about what kind of thing one is.

# The eight-byte header the daemon puts in front of every chunk of a

# it is named here: one byte of stream, three of padding, four of length.

# What it may take of the machine. Written here rather than in a

        # and because a template that could choose its own limits could choose
        # none (D86).

# Stamped rather than derived from `connector_id`, which goes null

        # service that never got this far from one whose connection is gone

# The database is up and usable; only the demonstration content
            # is missing. Said as a failure of the creation all the same,
            # because a person who asked for something to look at and got an
            # empty server would otherwise have to work out why themselves.

# What the runtime says about a service's container, plus the answer for a
# server that could not ask at all. Separate from `state`, which is what this
# application believes: the two disagreeing is exactly what a person needs to
# see.

# What the request that made it called itself, when it called itself
