    # double press, a retried POST — and answers with this row rather than
    # starting a second container (D84).

# The credential slots the requester named themselves, as the template's
    # own field names. A JSON column and never a secret: a typed password goes
    # in the encrypted column below rather than in here, so nothing in this
    # one has to be treated as a secret at all (D4).

# When this service became a connection. Kept after the connector itself
    # is deleted, which is the whole reason it exists: `connector_id` going
    # null then looks exactly like a creation that never got that far, and a
    # running database would be offered a retry that would destroy it (D84).

# Whether this service ever became a connection. With `connector_id` it
    # tells the two empty cases apart: one that never got that far, and one
    # whose connection its owner has since deleted. Only the first may be
    # started over; the second is a database somebody is still using (D84).

# What a name in somebody's own database server may look like. Letters,
# digits and underscores, starting with a letter — the intersection of what
# PostgreSQL accepts unquoted and what survives being an environment variable
# in a container's specification, which is where these two values go.

# What a container that is a program rather than a service is marked
# with. It lives and dies inside one job, so it never appears in a sweep
# for orphans — but a person reading `docker ps` mid-backup should still
# be able to tell what it is.

# Which of the template's shapes this service took: with a password, or
    # without one where the template allows that. Carried rather than worked
    # out again, because the connector must be described the same way the
    # container was started.

# What the ready service becomes, in both the name routes use and the
    # words the adapter calls itself by. Sent rather than joined on the client
    # against the adapter-types list: one name for a source type, and it is
    # the server's.

# Whether this server could actually start one now, and why not when it
    # could not. Said where the offer is made rather than only when the button
    # is pressed: a screen that offers what will be refused is a screen that
    # lies (D82).

# Refused here rather than by a constraint on the field: a failed
            # constraint puts the value it rejected into the validation error,
            # and a 422 body echoing somebody's password is the thing
            # `SecretStr` is there to prevent.

# Where a service published on this machine answers. The container is bound to
# the loopback address, so this is the only address that reaches it — and it is
# the address as seen from the machine the server runs on, which is what a
# person pasting it into their own tool needs.

# One variant so far, so this is the variant itself. A second kind of tab makes
# it `Annotated[RowsView | ChartView, Field(discriminator="kind")]`, which is a
# change of this line and of nothing that stores or carries a body: `kind` is
# already written, already required and already checked.

<!-- The heading names the page and the list names the section: a header
         that repeated the section would be saying it twice, and AppPageHeader
         takes a title and nothing else. -->

<!-- The question follows the action's declaration rather than a list of
           destructive action names kept by the client. It stays ordinary text:
           the target name is the useful part of this confirmation. -->

<!-- What was chosen, before any of it is sent. Choosing a file only
           puts it here, so a list that is wrong is corrected by taking a
           row out of it: that file never leaves the browser. -->

<!-- Drawn while there is anything to offer, which is now either the source's
       actions or the client's own verbs: a source with no actions at all still
       describes its nodes. -->

<!-- The hint is only on a caption that says nothing was counted: one
             word stands for a table nobody has analysed and for a view with
             no rows to count, and the column has room for neither reason. -->

<!-- Read-only, and in the editor everything else in this application
           reads code in: the language follows the name of the file the source
           would have saved. -->

<!-- Only for a dialect something draws. The file is what the site
           takes, so the door is offered beside Copy and Save rather than
           instead of them. -->

<!-- No way back to a catalog: a chart is drawn from a page of rows and
         is not a view of a node, so it offers no button rather than one that
         does nothing (D112). -->

<!-- Offered only where this server has a template for the type, and
           disabled with the server's own reason where it has one and cannot
           use it: a button that would be refused is worse than no button. -->

<!-- The tail that points at the button below, as in a speech bubble: what
         makes the panel belong to that button rather than float over the
         form. -->

<!-- A div and not a button: the row carries the icon button that opens the
         window, and a button inside a button is markup no browser agrees
         about. -->

<!-- The icon carries the state dot, exactly as it does in the strip a
           collapsed column leaves behind: what a press means differs, what is
           drawn does not. -->

<!-- Only for a connection that exists: there is nothing to switch
               off before it is saved, and the row would ask a question about
               a thing that is not there yet. -->

<!-- The result of the last check floats over this strip rather than
           sitting in the form: it is read once and dismissed, and a line in
           the body moved every field below it. -->

<!-- The element's own failure is shown rather than swallowed: the
           container was verified, its codecs were not, and whether this
           browser can play them is its answer to give (D52). -->

<!-- Above the banner rather than inside the branch that draws a document:
         a document that failed to load is exactly when re-reading it is worth
         offering, and the row that offers it must be on screen to be pressed. -->

<!-- Which side the icon is on is part of what the button says: one
               before the label names the action, one after it points where
               the action goes. -->

<!-- Hidden where there is nothing to choose: every column of a
               delimited file is text, and a list of one is a control that
               does nothing but take up the line (D45). -->

<!-- The opposite corner for the opposite direction: what points at this
           row. A menu rather than a jump, because there is usually more than
           one answer and only the reader knows which one they meant (D110). -->

<!-- Three places, one of which is always the one you are in. As two
         toggles they overlapped: Trash did nothing while History was showing,
         and had to be greyed out to say so. -->

<!-- The one command that puts this console into the library. Until it
           is pressed the text is in this tab and nowhere else, which is why
           the button says what it does rather than "Save". -->

<!-- Everything the server knows about it, which is the reason this is
             a window rather than a strip in a column: what it is, what runs
             it, and when it was made. -->

<!-- Offered for as long as the service exists: an address and the names
           it goes by are not a secret, so there is nothing to ration. Whatever
           was made up here is not in the answer (D89). -->

<!-- Only where running without one is a configuration rather than a
             mistake. A PostgreSQL that trusts every connection is not a
             service this server will start, so it is never offered. -->

<!-- Only where there is no page already showing it: opened from
               the connection's own window, the list is behind this dialog and
               a second copy of it would be a second answer (D33). -->

<!-- Where there is no page showing them: from a tab this dialog is
             the only place the owner has, and from the connection's own
             window they are on the page behind it (D61). -->

<!-- Said once, as a property of changing a type at all: which pairs lose
           what is PostgreSQL's rule, and restating it here would be a second
           implementation of it. -->

<!-- The fact being changed is already printed here, so it is the
               control: another icon in the row of actions would have to name
               in a tooltip which of a column's facts it changes. -->

<!-- Greyed out rather than hidden, for the reason the catalog's menu is:
         a bar that changes shape as the user walks about is a bar they have to
         read every time. The tooltip is where the reason is. -->

<!-- On the right, away from the commands of the open connection: this one
         is about the machine, and a button whose subject is different from
         its neighbours' should not sit in the same row of them. -->

<!-- `display: contents`, so the buttons join the row they are dropped into
       rather than forming a group of their own inside it: the gaps a toolbar
       sets between its buttons then hold across the join. -->

<!-- The trail scrolls and the home button does not: a path deep
               enough to run out of the column must not carry away the one
               step that always gets back. -->

<!-- Outside the trail, like the home button and for the same
               reason: a path deep enough to scroll must not carry away the
               one control that takes it somewhere. -->

<!-- One menu, fed from wherever the selection lives: a level's ticks
             or a tree's one selected node. What an action may do to them is
             still the server's answer about those nodes. -->

<!-- The same test id the wide panel carries, because it is the same
         action: the strip and the panel stand under v-if/v-else in the
         section and never exist at the same time. -->

<!-- At the end of the row, where every panel keeps what it offers about
           itself. The list of connections is nobody's node, so re-reading it
           is the only thing here (D112). -->

<!-- A row of one group: the view below is a stack of sections and offers
         nothing about the panel itself, so what the panel offers stands on a
         line of its own (D112). -->

<!-- A real button, and not "press the plus on the left": sending
               somebody to look for a control elsewhere on the screen when it
               can be given here is worse than giving it. -->

<!-- No standing bar under the canvas: it counted what is already on
         screen and listed the gestures, and the canvas itself carries those
         in the label a reader hears. -->

<!-- The one control with no line under it: a toggle's label is
             already the whole statement — "Replace it if it already exists" —
             and a model that wants to say more says it there. -->

<!-- choices is optional on FieldSpec, and the untyped q-select used to
           accept undefined without a word. A select shows no example: what a
           filled one looks like is the list it offers. -->

<!-- A field with an example keeps its label above the box: Quasar hides a
         placeholder until the label floats, and a floating label is exactly
         what sits where the example would be. -->

<!-- Forwarded rather than left to fall through: a slot does not fall
         through at all, so a search field had no way to carry its magnifier
         except by going around the kit. -->

<!-- Keep companion actions in the field's 56px marginal area, above the
         separately reserved error-message line. AppInput exposes the same
         contract, so screens never compensate for QField geometry themselves. -->

<!-- Where the tab in the hand would land. Drawn before the tab it
               would come before, and after the last one when it goes at the
               end, so the strip says what the release will do. -->

# Settings validation normally makes this unreachable. Keeping the
        # assembly boundary explicit makes a partially constructed Settings
        # double fail closed as well.

# Emptying query Trash is the one thing here that is not a resource: it is
    # a timer, and it belongs to the application for the same reason a pool
    # does — nothing else outlives a request.

# Serving the built frontend is enabled only when a build exists: without the
# check app.frontend raises RuntimeError and the application stops importing,
# including in tests, which do not need a build.

# Two, because two is what makes the point: one line crosses from a database
# to a file in personal storage, and one joins two files that only a person
# knows belong together.

# Two seconds of real H.264 in an MP4, for the same reason the PNG is real: a
# hand-built container verifies and then fails in the player, which is a worse
# sample than none. 1.8 KB, encoded here because nothing binary is committed.

# A log, which reads as text and opens as a table of the columns its own
    # lines are written in. Two continuation lines, because a real log has
    # them and they are what a naive parser drops.

# Every node whose children changed. None means the root of the connector.
    # A move names both parents; making the client infer either one from the
    # moved node's opaque id would break D21.

# Why an action that is understood must still not be performed. Kept apart
# from AdapterError, which means the source itself failed: a taken name is not
# a failure of the file system, and answering 502 for it would be a lie.

# Which kinds of catalog node the action makes sense for. Whether it is
    # allowed on one particular node — the root of a connector, say — is a
    # question of state and belongs to the driver.

# True when the action cannot be performed as the form now stands. A
    # statement rather than an error: the request to look was answered, and
    # what it says is that the other request would not be.

# The longest window a connection's owner may ask for. A day is far past any
# staleness somebody browsing data would accept, and a ceiling means a typo of
# one extra zero cannot pin a page there for a week (D105).

# Every member of the closed set is named. A sixth status added to
        # CacheStatus fails the type check here rather than being counted
        # silently as something it is not.

# How long ago the source was actually read, in seconds. Zero whenever
    # this call is the read, and the entry's age on a hit: what the caller
    # wants to say is how old the data is, not when the cache was asked.

# Which one the connection itself names, and therefore the one the catalog
    # opens on. Said by the source, because only the source knows what its
    # connection was written with.

# Seconds until it disappears, or nothing when it will not. Read at the
    # moment of listing, and therefore already out of date — which is why it
    # is a caption rather than anything a decision is made from.

# How many of whatever it holds: characters of a string, fields of a hash,
    # members of a set. One number, because "how big is it" is one question
    # however the answer is counted.

# The results whose bytes arrive through the ranged route rather than in the
# answer itself. One tuple, so the route that mints a ticket and the test that
# checks every streamable representation cannot drift apart.

# True when the text held more rows than the ceiling allows. What to do
    # about that belongs to the caller: paging a file and loading one are not
    # the same answer.

# Empty for a source that has no such notion at all; a source that has
    # references but no capability to follow them cannot arise, because the
    # same module answers both.

# Filled by the connector route from the facade's optional capability.
    # A capability belongs to the composed adapter, not to the fetch module
    # that produced this page.

# How often the source thinks this relation is worth reading again, when
    # it has an opinion. A list of server processes is about what is happening
    # this second; a table of invoices is not, and says nothing (D67).

# What may be done with this page beyond reading it. Everything, unless
    # the source says otherwise: a page is ordinarily somebody's own data, and
    # only a source knows when it is not (D72).

# The closed class of one prepared statement. "unknown" is a refusal rather
# than a write-shaped guess: a statement whose class cannot be established is
# not run (D62).

# The five below are filled in from what the adapter actually implements,
    # by the route that answers this. An adapter does not restate them, so a
    # capability cannot be announced and then be missing (D62).

# Whether what it does cannot be read back out of the statement: a drop, a
    # truncation, an alter that takes something away. These are rehearsed in a
    # transaction that is rolled back before they are run (D66).

# What this statement changed about the structure, named by the source.
    # It is a promise about what would be true once the transaction it ran in
    # commits, so a caller applies it then and never after a rollback (D66).

# Filled in on the way out, by the route rather than by the source that
    # answered. Null only inside the application, never in a reply: a declared
    # reference can land in another connection entirely (D108).

# Built by the source against the target's own columns, in the same closed
    # vocabulary any other filter uses, so the fetch it is handed to validates
    # it exactly as it validates a filter a user typed.

# What kind of thing a source is, for the one screen that groups them. A
# closed set rather than a free string: a category is a set of values, so a
# typo has to fail to compile instead of quietly creating a group of one.

# What sort of statement a capability makes: what can be looked at, and what
# can be changed. Two rather than the old application's ten, because two is
# what the derivation below can honestly tell apart.

# A model, or a discriminated union of them when the fields depend on
    # the way the source is connected to. Everything that reads it goes
    # through `app.adapters.options`, which answers for both.

# The driver class, kept beside the factory that builds instances of it.
    # Capabilities are a question about the type — no connector exists yet, so
    # there are no options and no session to build an instance from.

# A constraint added NOT VALID promises nothing about the rows that were
    # already there. Showing it as if it did would be a lie the reader has no
    # way to catch.

# The exact subset behind the broad gate. Existing relational adapters
    # offer all six; a delimited file can change its header without claiming
    # defaults, nullability or source types it does not have.

# Rejected values are the same answer they are for an insert, and the same
# model: the reason a value cannot cross is the column's type either way, and
# a second shape for it would only be a second thing to keep in step.

# One lock for the whole store rather than one per key: creating an
        # entry does not talk to anything remote — a pool with min_size 0
        # connects on first use — so the section is short.

# How this source's catalog is best shown: walked one level at a time, or
    # expanded in place. A property of the source, so the screen reads it
    # instead of branching on the type's name (D62).

# What it will do, in the source's words. The client shows it and never
    # writes one of its own: a sentence about terminating a backend belongs
    # with the statement that terminates it.

# The column whose value names a row for this command. One column, because
    # that is what every command that exists needs; a compound key is a
    # different contract and is not invented before somebody has one.

# What a search may be asked for at most, and what it costs when nothing says.
# Named here and used by both the model and the route that fills it, so a
# ceiling is one number rather than two that agree today.

# How much of the line a match was found on is shown. A log line or a minified
# document is one line and can be enormous; what a reader needs is enough of it
# to recognise the hit.

# The line the words were found on, for a search that looked inside. A name
    # search leaves it empty: what matched is the name, and it is already the
    # row. Bounded by the source, because a log line can be a megabyte long.

# What the bytes turned out to be, rather than what the name promised. A file
# that is not UTF-8 says so instead of being decoded with replacements and
# called text.

# Why the counts above are absent. A stated ceiling beats a guessed count,
    # and every counting member here carries the same field for the same
    # reason.

# Both absent together with the reason: a file that was not read through
    # has a header and a width, and stating zero would be a count rather than
    # the silence it is.

# Estimated on purpose, as everywhere else this number is given: an exact
    # count costs a full scan, and the name says so rather than pairing a
    # number with a flag about how true it is.

# An entry too, because a file inside an archive is exactly what a reader
    # wants out of it (D53); everything that changes a node keeps to the two
    # kinds that exist on disk.

# Both ends change: the folder that gained the nodes, and — for a move
        # — every folder that lost one. Named by the server, because deriving
        # them from the action's name is the rule this exists to avoid.

# A nested value arrives as Python containers. It is serialised here
        # and compacted by the shared renderer, so JSON has one spelling
        # wherever it crosses the boundary (D23).

# Arrow hands an interval over as a named tuple, whose repr is the
        # name of a Python class. ISO 8601 is the one spelling of a duration
        # that says what it is without a reader knowing the library.

# A container is opened once here, and what is inside it becomes
            # nodes of its own (D51, D53). This is the one place a file is read
            # while listing, and it happens because the user asked for it.

# A whole JSON document has no honest partial tree, so it is parsed only below
# this ceiling. Above it the JSON viewer keeps its identity and shows a bounded
# source preview with the reason instead.

# Editing is a whole-document operation: both the source shown to the user and
# the replacement have to fit this ceiling. Larger files keep their bounded
# viewer and name why the editor cannot write them.

# An entry is expanded into a bounded temporary file and read by the
        # ordinary viewer, which is what lets every one of them work inside an
        # archive without a second implementation (D53).

# Why each class other than `read` will not run here. One sentence each, naming
# the family rather than the statement, because the answer is about what this
# source is and not about what somebody typed (D77).

# The engine could not read the text as statements at all. That is one
        # unknown statement spanning what was sent, so the console marks the
        # place rather than showing nothing.

# A file has no index to order by, and ordering one page of it would be
        # ordering the page rather than the file. Looking a value up is a scan
        # the source can do honestly, and does (D109).

# Expanded into a temporary file and read like any other, so a
                # table inside an archive needs no second reader (D53). Paging
                # expands it once per page, which is what the ceiling is for.

# Classification is intentionally by name in the catalog: inspecting every
# entry would cost one open per file. The content reader checks the bytes when
# that one node is actually opened.

# A text file has no columns of its own, so numbering its lines
            # was a table in name only. It is offered as source, and nothing
            # else.

# An archive, a font, a legacy document: still listed, still
            # downloadable, and honest about having no viewer rather than
            # opening something that cannot be shown.

# Which representations are the source of a document rather than a rendering
# of it. Everything here is served by the one editor route, so a format that
# offers any of them has text to show.

# How many lines are read to decide what a file is. Enough that a run of
# stack-trace lines at the top cannot speak for the file, small enough that
# deciding costs nothing.

# How much of the sample a shape has to fit before it is believed. Not all of
# it: a real log holds continuation lines, blank lines and the occasional line
# written by something else.

# The shapes, most particular first: a PostgreSQL line also satisfies the
# looser "time, level, message" of the plain shape, and being told it is a
# PostgreSQL log is worth more than being told it is a log.

# ISO base media files hold their index in `moov`, which may sit at the end.
# The boxes are walked by their own sizes, so what is read is one header per

# One entry, and it is not a choice: a delimited file states no types and every
# value read out of one comes back as text (D45). Published all the same,
# because the screen asks the container what it accepts rather than knowing.

# Containment first, as every read of this source judges it (D8). The
        # root itself is a folder and is named by the empty id, which is what

# The only option there is. The root itself is never named by the client:

# How a tar is opened for writing, per format. `w` is no compression at all.
# Typed as the literals `tarfile.open` declares, so a mode that is not one of

# How many rows come out of the file at a time while it is being searched. Only

# What the engine is allowed to take while it works. A file source is one

# How far the editor's list of relations may look, and how much of it it may

# A drive letter or a path starting at the root: what a message must never

# ids exist to hide (D78).

# What every engine starts with, before it is given anything. Extensions are
# neither installed nor loaded, so a statement cannot reach the network by
# asking for a reader that would arrive over it.

# Said by the caller only where the name cannot say it: a log whose

# One JSON document is only valid whole, so the reading cannot be cut short at

# request bounded; above it the file is still readable, as lines.

# The categories a JSON value can land in, which is a closed set smaller than
# the one a source may declare: an unlisted one has to fail to type check here

# One reason for all three gates: nothing about the shape of a file dataset is

# A folder that cannot be read is not a failed search: the rest

# Complete about what it read, and honest about what it did not: a

# What is read to count lines or rows. Well above the 4 MB a document is edited

# A sheet has no bytes and no times of its own; the workbook has both,

# A log is text as far as this is concerned: how many lines, what

# A font, an executable, a legacy document: the facts every file

# A workbook is a zip, so its size on disk says nothing about what opening it

# Unreachable while every column is text, and answered rather than

# What a refused drop means, by SQLSTATE. The code is safe to look at and the

# What a relation is dropped by, and the order the commands are issued in.
# A view is dropped before the table it reads, so that selecting both succeeds

# One transaction, so a selection that cannot be dropped whole leaves

# A screen of its own rather than a form: the answer is a document, and

# A report admits a command when the command is about what it reports,

# A report has no DDL — there is nothing on the server to recreate — but it
# does have the statement it is made of, and that is the same question a
# person asks of a table when they open its DDL: what is this, really.

# An id in the reports' namespace naming no report is gone rather than

        # because PostgreSQL reserves the prefix.

# What a refused type change means, by SQLSTATE. The code is safe to look at
# and the message beside it is not: PostgreSQL writes the offending value into

# Composing the literal is what would fail, and it fails with a
            # driver error rather than with a rejected value. Said here, it is

# Nothing has been locked and nothing has been altered: the
                # count is the whole answer, and the caller decides what to do
                # about the rows.

# The closed vocabulary of what happens to a referencing row. It is the same
# set the relation model already reports, so nothing new is invented; each is
# written out as a literal fragment rather than composed from the value.

# datatype_mismatch and undefined_function: the two column lists cannot be

    # fails at the constraint or at the count that precedes it.

# A value that cannot be read is the same failure whichever route reaches it,
# and the sentence is all that can honestly be said when the check itself is
# the thing that failed.

# An ALTER is asked for every table it names, so a rename reaches both

# A limit of one exists only to reuse the page query's validation
        # object. It never reaches the export statement, which has no limit or
        # offset at all.
